title: Emotion Vocabulary
keyIdea: There are many more feeling words than happy, sad, angry and scared. Some words are the same feeling at a different strength, like annoyed and furious. Some sound alike but mean different things: scared is about danger now, worried is about what might happen later. You can feel two things at once. The more exact the word, the better other people understand you.

kid: Happy, sad, angry and scared are a good start. But there are lots more feeling words. Proud, grateful, lonely, jealous, worried and embarrassed are a few of them.
Some words are one feeling at different sizes. Annoyed is a small anger. Cross is a bit more. Angry is big. Furious is the biggest. Pick the size that fits.

Some words are close cousins. Scared is about danger right now. Worried is about what might happen later. Lonely is when you want a friend near you. Alone just means no one is with you. You can be alone and happy.

Proud is when you did something good. Grateful is when someone was kind to you. Guilty is when you did something wrong. Embarrassed is when people see a silly moment. You can feel two things at once, too, like excited and nervous on a first day.
adult: By around seven to nine, children are ready to move past the basic feelings to a wider set of words, and to tell close words apart. Research on emotional granularity suggests that people who name feelings precisely cope with them better, and a school programme built around feeling words was linked to better grades and social skills.

The lab works on four skills. Children rank anger words by strength on a thermometer. They sort close pairs by the clue that separates them: now or later for scared and worried, wanting company for lonely and alone, doing wrong or being seen for guilty and embarrassed. They put two feelings into one jar for mixed moments, then find every word that fits a child left out of a party.

A common mistake is using one big word for every size of feeling, so a small upset becomes I am furious. Another is mixing up close words, such as calling embarrassment guilt, or thinking that being alone always means feeling lonely. Children also often believe you can only feel one thing at a time. Be careful not to correct a child's feeling itself; offer a sharper word for it.

At home, when your child says sad or angry, offer two exact words and let them choose: do you feel left out, or disappointed? Name your own mixed feelings out loud too, so they hear that it is normal.

familyTip: When your child says I feel sad or I feel angry, ask which kind: a small one or a big one? Offer two exact words, like left out or disappointed, and let them choose. Share your own feeling words too.

practice.prompt: Someone hums while you read. It goes on for {n} minutes. It is not a big deal, just a bit irritating. Which word fits best?
practice.hint: Is this a small feeling or a huge one? Pick the word that fits the size.
practice.explain: Annoyed is a small anger. Humming for {n} minutes is irritating, but furious would be far too big.

practice.prompt: Tom has a spelling test in {n} days. He keeps thinking about it at bedtime. Which word fits best?
practice.hint: Is the danger right here now, or is it something that might happen later?
practice.explain: Worried is about what might happen later. The test is {n} days away, so Tom is worried, not scared.

practice.prompt: Ava is drawing on her own in her room and loving it. Which word fits best?
practice.hint: Does Ava want someone to be with her right now?
practice.explain: Ava is alone, but she does not want company, so she is not lonely. Being alone and happy is fine.

practice.prompt: Leo spilt paint on his friend's picture and did not say sorry. Which word fits best?
practice.hint: Did Leo do something wrong, or was he just seen in a silly moment?
practice.explain: Guilty is the feeling after you did something wrong. Saying sorry can help it pass.

practice.prompt: It is the first day at a new club. Zara has butterflies but wants to go. Which pair fits best?
practice.hint: Can one moment bring two feelings at once?
practice.explain: Zara is both excited and nervous. Two feelings at once is normal.

pool.prompt: Which list goes from the mildest feeling to the strongest?
pool.hint: Start with a small fed-up feeling and end with the very biggest anger.
pool.explain: Annoyed is the mildest, then cross, then angry, and furious is the strongest.

pool.prompt: A big dog runs at you barking. Which word fits best?
pool.hint: Is the danger happening right now?
pool.explain: Scared is about danger right now. Worried is about something that might happen later.

pool.prompt: Kai has no one to play with in a busy playground and wishes he did. Which word fits best?
pool.hint: Does Kai want someone to be with him?
pool.explain: Lonely means wanting company. You can feel lonely even with lots of people around.

pool.prompt: You practised piano for {n} weeks and played the hard piece with no mistakes. Which word fits best?
pool.hint: Who did the good thing here: you, or someone else?
pool.explain: Proud is the feeling when you did something good, like {n} weeks of practice paying off.

pool.prompt: A neighbour helped you look for your lost cat for {n} hours. Which word fits best?
pool.hint: Did you do something good, or did someone do something kind for you?
pool.explain: Grateful is how you feel when someone does something kind for you, like searching for {n} hours.

pool.prompt: You tripped on stage and people laughed, but you did nothing wrong. Which word fits best?
pool.hint: Did you do something wrong, or did people see an awkward moment?
pool.explain: Embarrassed is about being seen in an awkward moment. Guilty is for doing something wrong.

pool.prompt: Mia was not invited to a party. Which answer says most about how she feels?
pool.hint: Which answer gives the most exact words?
pool.explain: Sad is true but blurry. Left out and disappointed tell people exactly what kind of sad it is.

pool.prompt: Your friend got the new game you really wanted. Which word fits best?
pool.hint: Which word means wanting something that someone else has got?
pool.explain: Jealous is wanting what someone else has got. It is a normal feeling, and naming it helps.

visual.caption: Small feeling or big feeling? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: rank anger words on a thermometer, sort close cousins, mix two feelings in a jar and find the exact word.
